html:
The Swahili city-states were Muslim trading towns along the coast of East Africa, from southern Somalia to Mozambique, among them Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Lamu and Zanzibar. They flourished from about the 10th century until Portuguese attacks in the early 16th.

The towns grew out of Bantu-speaking farming and fishing villages, part of the long Bantu expansion, that joined the trade of the Indian Ocean. Merchants from Arabia, Persia and India came on the monsoon winds, married into local families and settled. The result was a distinct culture: the Swahili language is a Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords, and "Swahili" itself comes from the Arabic for "coasts". Islam became the faith of the towns' elites from the 8th to 12th centuries.

What they traded:

  • Out: gold from inland, especially from the Great Zimbabwe region by way of the port of Sofala, along with ivory, mangrove timber and enslaved people.
  • In: Indian cotton cloth, glass beads, and Chinese porcelain, which was set into the walls and tombs of the richest houses.

Each town was independent, ruled by its own sultan or council, and they often competed. Kilwa was the richest in the 14th century; Ibn Battuta visited it in 1331 and called it one of the most beautiful towns in the world. Its Great Mosque and the palace of Husuni Kubwa are built of coral stone. In 1418 Malindi received Zheng He's fleet.

In 1498 Vasco da Gama found a pilot at Malindi to guide him to India. The Portuguese came back to sack Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505 and took control of the coast's trade. Oman later drove the Portuguese out, and the coast's history passed to the Omani sultans of Zanzibar.
